title: Black Holes
subtitle: A window on extreme gravity
description: Interactive walk through event horizons, Schwarzschild scale, approach regions, illustrative lensing, accretion appearance, tidal forces, EHT imaging of M87* and Sgr A*, Cygnus X-1, and how astronomers detect black holes.
source_note: Scale, approach, and lensing labs are ILLUSTRATIVE. Schwarzschild numbers assume non-rotating models unless noted. EHT images are interferometric reconstructions. Stellarium is sky context only.

steps.title: The darkest objects
steps.narration_text: Black holes are regions where spacetime curvature prevents light from escaping beyond an event horizon. This walk separates observation, reconstruction, simulation, illustration, and theoretical models.

steps.title: Gravity without escape
steps.narration_text: A black hole is defined by causal structure—not a solid crust. Rubber-sheet metaphors are only metaphors.

steps.title: The event horizon
steps.narration_text: The horizon is a boundary in spacetime. The singularity of classical general relativity is not directly imaged. The Event Horizon Telescope shadow is larger than the horizon itself.

steps.title: How big is a black hole?
steps.narration_text: Compare stellar-mass and supermassive Schwarzschild radii. Real astrophysical black holes may rotate—labels state the non-rotating teaching assumption.

steps.title: Falling toward the horizon
steps.narration_text: Move through distant space, the accretion region, the photon-orbit region, and the event horizon. The photon sphere is not a solid shell, and you cannot hover freely at the horizon.

steps.title: Light bends
steps.narration_text: Near a black hole, light paths bend. This lab is illustrative relativistic lensing—not a precision ray-tracer—while EHT images reconstruct real interferometric data.

steps.title: Accretion and the glowing disk
steps.narration_text: Bright disks and jets live outside the horizon. Doppler boosting, gravitational redshift, and light bending shape appearance in ray-traced visualizations.

steps.title: Tidal forces
steps.narration_text: Spaghettification is not universal at every horizon. Stellar-mass tides near the horizon can be extreme; for large supermassive black holes, local tides at the horizon can be gentler.

steps.title: Sgr A* — our Galactic Center
steps.narration_text: Sagittarius A-star is the Milky Way’s central supermassive black hole. Stellarium anchors near the Galactic Center using NGC 6522 as honest host-sky context—not a fake Sgr A-star catalog object.

steps.title: M87* — seeing the shadow
steps.narration_text: M87-star gave us the first horizon-scale image in 2019. The dark center is a reconstructed shadow shaped by light bending—not a photograph of a black surface.

steps.title: Stellar-mass black holes
steps.narration_text: Cygnus X-1 is a classic stellar-mass black-hole X-ray binary. Stellarium focuses the optical companion HD 226868—sky context for the system, not a resolved black-hole image.

steps.title: How we know they’re there
steps.narration_text: We find black holes through stellar orbits, X-ray binaries, gravitational waves, Galactic-Center dynamics, and Event Horizon Telescope imaging. Visit the Gravitational Waves Special for chirps and mergers.

steps.title: A window on extreme gravity
steps.narration_text: Black holes reshape light and matter around them. Distinguishing illustration from reconstruction keeps the science honest. Exit and Restore returns Stellarium when you are done.
